item.title: How the Dirty Set Moves: Characterizing Schedule Reuse in Incremental Sparse Matrix Multiplication
item.description: arXiv:2610.19489v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sparse matrices, in which most entries are zero, are central to scientific simulation, graph analytics and machine learning, and their multiplication with dense inputs is a core parallel kernel. In many applications the matrix stays fixed while only a few input rows change per step, so the result can be updated from those rows alone, which we call the dirty set. Sparse kernels often add a second optimization based on the inspector-executor principle, in which a tiled schedule is prepared once and reused across calls. However, when this reuse remains profitable as the dirty set moves is not well characterized. In this paper, we show that retained tiled execution rarely beats direct CSC in incremental sparse matrix multiplication, although incremental execution itself remains highly profitable. Across 21 SuiteSparse matrices and controlled patterns of motion, a direct column-wise incremental update is 2.1-8.2x faster than the best of eight full-recomputation codes, among them Intel oneMKL and PyTorch. Yet the same direct update outperforms a tiled executor that retains tile preparation and caches assembled schedules in 779 of 837 workloads. Separating reuse into per-tile preparation and cached schedules shows that the benefit comes from preparation; extra cache capacity seldom helps because a tile set rarely returns after a different one has intervened. Tiling is faster only when tiles merge many entries into each output write, a structural property that we predicted before measurement and confirmed on four held-out matrices of the same family. These results show that the structure of the matrix and the motion of the dirty set, rather than the sophistication of the schedule, determine whether reuse is profitable. We anticipate that our methodology and guidelines will help developers decide when to build schedule reuse into incremental sparse runtimes.
item.dc:creator: Hunter Horne (HorneSci), Eric Spencer (Loyola University Chicago, HorneSci), Alex Henningfield (HorneSci), Arslan Bisharat (Loyola University Chicago)

item.title: Lag: A Mean-Field Optimal Policy for Online Assignment with Reusable Resources
item.description: arXiv:2610.19038v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study online task assignment with reusable resources. This problem arises in peer reviewer assignment, skill-based call routing, rideshare matching, emergency dispatch, and crowdsourcing: Tasks arrive according to a geometric process and must be immediately assigned to servers that become temporarily busy, yielding rewards that depend on the task-server pair. The goal is to maximize long-run average reward. We cast the problem as a contextual restless multi-armed bandit (CRMAB). We derive an occupancy-measure LP (OCC-LP) that upper-bounds the reward of any work-conserving policy. From its dual we obtain Lag, a closed-form index policy. We introduce a scaling regime in which the number of copies of each server and the number of arrivals per step grow together. This regime yields the first deterministic fluid limit for a contextual bandit. In it, Lag is asymptotically optimal. Finally, we evaluate our algorithms on peer review datasets and call center routing. The Lagrangian index achieves 83-99% of the LP upper bound across all load levels. Moreover, the Lagrangian index policy significantly outperforms the natural greedy assignment scheme, improving reward by up to 12.3% on journal data and 36% on structured synthetic instances.
item.dc:creator: Keerthana Gurushankar

item.title: Learning in Strategic Queuing with Geometric Recharge: From Bandits to Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.19179v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study packet routing in queuing systems where queues act as selfish, myopic agents that use no-regret learning algorithms to select servers with unknown service rates. To model the small buffers used in data centers, we assume that each server has a single-packet buffer. Even such a tiny buffer already captures the features of buffering: routers can exploit multiple servers while accepted packets remain in service, but packets can occupy servers for multiple rounds, complicating future service and learning. We first analyze a single queue routing packets to $m$ buffered servers with service rates $\mu_1, \dots, \mu_m$. This setting is equivalent to an instance of the recharging bandits problem with geometric recharge. We prove that any no-regret learner achieves a long-run average throughput of at least the Hamacher sum of the server rates, and that this bound is tight. Consequently, a single no-regret queue is stable if and only if its arrival rate is below the Hamacher sum of the server rates. Moreover, comparing against an optimal policy, we show that any no-regret learner is at least $0.77$-competitive, which is also tight. We then study multi-queue systems where $n$ queues with arrival rates $\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n$, each at most $\lambda_{\max}$, compete for service from $m$ buffered servers. We show that the smallest overprovisioning factor that guarantees the system to be stable under high-probability no-regret learning is $\frac{1}{1-\lambda_{\max}}$. Equivalently, in terms of the total arrival and service rates, the condition $\sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i < (1-\lambda_{\max})\sum_{j=1}^m \mu_j$ is sufficient, and sometimes necessary, for stability under no-regret learning. In particular, for $\lambda_{\max} = 1/2$, this improves the upper bound of Abel et al. (EC 2026) from $3$ to $2$, matching their lower bound and resolving their open question.
item.dc:creator: Cristian Palma Foster, Eva Tardos

item.title: Scaling LLM Inference via Parallelism: Throughput-Latency Trade-off
item.description: arXiv:2610.19405v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) serving systems must balance latency and throughput while efficiently utilizing distributed GPU resources. This challenge arises because inference consists of two fundamentally different phases: prefill, which determines time-to-first-token (TTFT), and decode, which determines inter-token latency (ITL). The use of tensor parallelism (TP), pipeline parallelism (PP), and hybrid configurations exposes different trade-offs between these latency dimensions, making the optimal parallelism configuration highly dependent on workload characteristics, latency requirements, and context length. Moreover, despite the widespread adoption of distributed inference, there is still limited understanding of how parallelism configurations should be selected under varying workload conditions and service-level objectives (SLO). In this paper, we develop a systematic framework for characterizing LLM inference parallelism via throughput-latency trade-offs, SLO-aware serving, and long-context scalability. We introduce the notion of parallelism operating regions by constructing TTFT-ITL feasible sets and Pareto frontiers across different workload compositions, thereby revealing a systematic transition from TP-dominant to PP-dominant configurations as workloads become increasingly prefill-heavy. We further formulate SLO-aware parallelism selection using goodput, showing that stringent TTFT requirements favor PP-dominated configurations, whereas relaxed latency constraints progressively shift the optimality toward TP-dominated configurations with higher serving capacity. Finally, we demonstrate that increasing context length fundamentally changes the relative advantages of parallelism configurations, with PP-dominant configurations exhibiting more favorable scalability and SLO attainment in the long-context regime.
item.dc:creator: Javad Mirzaei, Jeebak Mitra

item.title: Delta Tokenizer: Reference-Identical Tokenization of Session Deltas and Segment-Parallelism for Long Prompts on Multicore CPUs
item.description: arXiv:2610.19801v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: An agent that drives an LLM sends the model the same conversation again and again, and each turn adds only a little text at the end. Inference engines reuse the KV cache of the shared prefix, so only the new tokens pass through the model. However, tokenization has no such shortcut. The CPU front end of the serving engine converts every request back into token IDs from its first character, which lengthens the time to first token (TTFT) and consumes CPU on every turn. We present Delta Tokenizer, a CPU tokenization front end that tokenizes only the delta between a request and the previous request of the same session. It retains the earlier token sequence, encodes again only the appended text and the short tail whose tokens the append could affect, and joins the two only at a position the tokenizer's splitting rules themselves cannot move, which keeps the result exact. For long requests with no state to reuse, it cuts the text where practical tokenizers already keep neighboring pieces independent, encodes the pieces on several cores at once, and concatenates the outputs into the reference encoding, exactly. A shared CPU pool schedules these chunks together with the short incremental updates, so an update runs between two chunks rather than behind an entire long job. The incremental path shortens the tokenization of a session turn by roughly 40x relative to the Hugging Face reference tokenizer, and on 16 cores the chunk-parallel path encodes a four-million-character request 8.2x faster than a serial encode and 1.6-2.1x faster than LoPT. Inside SGLang, Delta Tokenizer reduces the median TTFT through the chat interface by 59% at 100K tokens and brings the P99 TTFT of agent sessions down 9.5x under load and 23x when long requests tie up the front end. Every output we checked matches the reference, among them 41.8 billion documents encoded by its fast encoder.
item.dc:creator: Zhenyu Zhang, Zhichao Cao

item.title: Rethinking Sparse Formats for RISC-V: A Hierarchical Approach to High-Performance SpMV
item.description: arXiv:2609.11352v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The sparse matrix-vector multiplication (SpMV) algorithm is a fundamental computational kernel of linear algebra and serves as a building block for numerous applications, primarily iterative solvers for systems of linear equations used in scientific and engineering simulations. This paper compares vectorized implementations of the SpMV algorithm across eight established sparse matrix storage formats and proposes a novel modification of the CSR format, Hierarchical CSR (HCSR), which enhances SpMV performance on RISC-V processors. Our SpMV implementations utilize RVV 1.0 intrinsics and are publicly available as an open-source C++ library named RVVLASparse. Computational experiments conducted on SpacemiT K1 and K3 RISC-V boards demonstrate that the proposed HCSR format achieves the shortest execution time among all considered formats across a broad class of sparse matrices. HCSR outperforms the best CSR implementation on 8 cores, yielding an average speedup for double precision of 19% on K1 (13% on K3) and for single precision of 36% on K1 (34% on K3).
item.dc:creator: Anna Pirova, Anastasia Vodeneeva, Konstantin Kovalev, Alexander Ustinov, Maksim Zagriadskov, Daniil Litvyakov, Arthur Kulik, Evgeny Kozinov, Valentin Volokitin, Iosif Meyerov
